cx-axiom.title: Axiomatic definition: ℂ = (ℝ², +, ·)
cx-axiom.summary: A complex number is a pair of reals with a special multiplication rule. i² = −1 follows from it.
steps: A complex number is an ordered pair of real numbers (a, b). The first is the real part and the second the imaginary part.
Addition is done component by component, just like with vectors.
To guess what the product should be, we multiply (a + bi)(c + di) like two binomials: every term by every term (distributive property).
We use i² = −1, so bd·i² = −bd. Grouping: what has no i is the real part (ac − bd); what has i, the imaginary part (ad + bc).
That rule is exactly what's taken as the definition of the product of pairs. The symbol := means “is defined as”.
With this definition, i = (0, 1), and multiplying it by itself gives (−1, 0), which is the real number −1. So i² = −1 is no longer an “impossible number” but a consequence.
cx-axiom.use: Complex numbers are built from real numbers alone, no magic: they are points of the plane with a special way of multiplying.

cx-ipow.title: Powers of i
cx-ipow.summary: Powers of i repeat every 4: 1, i, −1, −i, 1, …
steps: Start from the definition: i squared is −1.
For i³ multiply by i once more: (−1)·i = −i.
i⁴ = i²·i² = (−1)(−1) = 1. We're back to the start.
Since every four powers we're back to 1, to compute iⁿ we only need the remainder r of dividing n by 4 (r = 0, 1, 2 or 3).
Example: 27 = 4·6 + 3, remainder 3. Since i⁴ = 1, (i⁴)⁶ = 1, leaving i³ = −i.
cx-ipow.use: Multiplying by i rotates 90° counterclockwise; four 90° turns make a full turn. That's why the cycle has length 4.

cx-field.title: ℂ is a field
cx-field.summary: Addition and multiplication follow the usual rules and every z ≠ 0 has an inverse.
steps: Addition and multiplication are commutative (order doesn't matter) and associative (grouping doesn't matter). They inherit this from ℝ.
The distributive property holds: multiplying by a sum is adding the products.
There are identity elements: 0 = 0 + 0i changes nothing when added, and 1 = 1 + 0i changes nothing when multiplied.
Every z has an opposite −z, which added to z gives 0.
Inverse: to make the denominator real, multiply top and bottom by a − bi (the conjugate). The bottom becomes a² + b², which is positive if z ≠ 0.
Example: the inverse of 1 + i is (1 − i)/2. Check: (1 + i)(1 − i)/2 = (1 − i²)/2 = 2/2 = 1.
cx-field.use: ℂ being a field means you can solve equations with complex numbers exactly like with real ones.

cx-order.title: Is 2 < i? No: ℂ can't be ordered
cx-order.summary: There is no order on ℂ compatible with its operations. Comparing complex numbers with < makes no sense.
steps: A “compatible” order (like the one on ℝ) must make the product of two positives positive.
Consequence: the square of any nonzero number is positive (if x < 0, then −x > 0 and x² = (−x)² > 0).
Suppose such an order exists on ℂ. Since i ≠ 0, we'd need i² > 0.
But i² = −1, so we'd get −1 > 0.
On the other hand, 1 = 1² is also a square, so 1 > 0.
Adding two positives (−1 and 1) must give a positive number: 0 > 0. That's impossible, so no such order exists.
cx-order.use: In ℂ you never say one number is bigger than another. What you can compare is their moduli |z| and |w|, which are real numbers.

cx-phasor.title: Phasor: a complex number of modulus 1
cx-phasor.summary: Complex numbers with |z| = 1 form the unit circle: they are the trigonometric circle.
steps: A phasor is a complex z with |z| = 1. Recall that |z| = √(a² + b²).
Squaring, |z| = 1 means a² + b² = 1, the equation of the circle of radius 1 centred at the origin.
Every point on that circle has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), as on the trigonometric circle.
So every phasor can be written z = cos θ + i sin θ, which is 1<sub>θ</sub> in polar form and e<sup>iθ</sup> in exponential form.
cx-phasor.use: Multiplying by a phasor rotates without changing size. In electricity they represent sinusoidal waves.

cx-conj1.title: The conjugate of the conjugate
cx-conj1.summary: Conjugating twice leaves the number as it was.
steps: Conjugating flips the sign of the imaginary part: a + bi becomes a − bi.
Conjugate again: the imaginary part is now −b, and we flip its sign once more.
−(−b) = b, so we get back a + bi = z.
cx-conj1.use: Geometrically, conjugating is reflecting across the real axis; reflecting twice leaves the point where it was.

cx-conj2.title: Conjugate of a sum
cx-conj2.summary: Adding then conjugating is the same as conjugating then adding.
steps: Write both numbers in rectangular form.
Add real parts to real parts and imaginary parts to imaginary parts.
Conjugate the result: flip the sign of the imaginary part.
Split it up: it's the sum of a − bi and c − di, that is, z̄ + w̄.
cx-conj2.use: It lets you conjugate long expressions term by term, for example when simplifying fractions.

cx-conj3.title: Conjugate of a product
cx-conj3.summary: The conjugate of a product is the product of the conjugates. In particular, conj(zⁿ) = z̄ⁿ.
steps: Product in rectangular form (definition of the product).
Conjugate it: only the sign of the imaginary part changes.
Now multiply the conjugates (a − bi)(c − di) term by term.
With i² = −1 we get (ac − bd) − (ad + bc)i: the same as in step 2.
A power is a repeated product, so applying the rule n times: conj(zⁿ) = (z̄)ⁿ.
cx-conj3.use: If a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex root z, it also has the root z̄: complex roots come in pairs.

cx-mod1.title: The modulus is ≥ 0 and only 0 at z = 0
cx-mod1.summary: |z| is a distance: never negative, and 0 only at the origin.
steps: The modulus is the distance from (a, b) to the origin: by Pythagoras, the hypotenuse with legs a and b.
a² and b² are squares, so they aren't negative; neither is their sum, nor its square root.
A sum of squares is 0 only if both squares are 0, that is, a = 0 and b = 0.
Example: |3 + 4i| = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 (the 3-4-5 triangle).
cx-mod1.use: The modulus measures the size of a complex number. It's what gets compared instead of the numbers themselves.

cx-tri.title: Triangle inequality
cx-tri.summary: The size of a sum never exceeds the sum of the sizes.
steps: z + w is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the arrows z and w (parallelogram rule).
To get from 0 to z + w we can go through z: first the arrow z (length |z|), then a copy of w (length |w|). That makes a triangle.
In a triangle, one side is never longer than the other two combined: the direct path is the shortest.
Equality only happens when z and w point the same way: the triangle flattens into a segment.
cx-tri.use: It gives bounds: if you know how big z and w are, you know at most how big z + w is.

cx-modprod.title: Modulus of a product
cx-modprod.summary: When multiplying complex numbers, the moduli multiply: |zw| = |z||w|.
steps: Apply the definition of modulus to the product zw = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.
Expand both squares. The terms −2abcd and +2abcd cancel.
Factor: a² multiplies (c² + d²) and so does b².
That's |z|²·|w|². Since moduli are ≥ 0, we can drop the squares.
A power is a repeated product, so |zⁿ| = |z|ⁿ.
cx-modprod.use: It's half of the polar product rule: sizes multiply (the other half: angles add).

cx-modconj.title: A number and its conjugate have the same size
cx-modconj.summary: |z| = |z̄|: reflecting doesn't change the distance to the origin.
steps: The conjugate of a + bi is a − bi.
When squaring, (−b)² = b², so the modulus is the same.
cx-modconj.use: z and z̄ are at the same distance from the origin, with opposite angles θ and −θ.

cx-zz.title: z · z̄ = |z|²
cx-zz.summary: A complex number times its conjugate is always a real number ≥ 0.
steps: Multiply z = a + bi by its conjugate a − bi.
Expand: the terms −abi and +abi cancel.
Since i² = −1, −b²i² = +b².
We're left with a² + b², the modulus squared: a real, non-negative number.
cx-zz.use: It's the trick for dividing: multiplying by the conjugate turns a complex number into a real one.

cx-div.title: Division: z/w = z·w̄ / |w|²
cx-div.summary: To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
steps: Multiply numerator and denominator by w̄. That's multiplying by w̄/w̄ = 1, so the value doesn't change.
The bottom becomes w·w̄ = |w|², a real number. Dividing by a real number is easy: divide each part.
Special case z = 1: the inverse of w is w̄/|w|².
Example: (2 + 3i)/(1 + 2i). The conjugate of 1 + 2i is 1 − 2i and |1 + 2i|² = 1² + 2² = 5.
Expand: 2 − 4i + 3i − 6i² = 2 + 6 − i = 8 − i. Divide each part by 5.
cx-div.use: That's how you divide in rectangular form. In polar form it's even easier: divide the moduli and subtract the angles.

cx-arg.title: From rectangular to polar (and the arctan trap)
cx-arg.summary: ρ = √(a² + b²) and θ = arctan(b/a), corrected by quadrant.
steps: In the triangle with legs a (horizontal) and b (vertical) and hypotenuse ρ, sine is opposite/hypotenuse and cosine is adjacent/hypotenuse.
Dividing, tan θ = b/a, so θ = arctan(b/a)… but only sometimes.
arctan only returns angles between −π/2 and π/2 (quadrants I and IV), which are the ones with a > 0. There the formula is right.
If a < 0 the point is on the left: b/a gives the same value for z and for −z (the opposite point), so we must correct by adding π (if b ≥ 0) or subtracting π (if b < 0).
If a = 0, b/a doesn't exist: the point is on the imaginary axis, θ = π/2 if b > 0 and −π/2 if b < 0.
arg (lowercase) is the set of all valid angles; Arg (capital) is the principal one, the only one in (−π, π].
cx-arg.use: Careful with calculators: arctan((−1)/(−1)) = π/4, but −1 − i is in the third quadrant and its Arg is −3π/4.

cx-p2b.title: From polar to rectangular
cx-p2b.summary: a = ρ cos θ and b = ρ sin θ. This gives the trigonometric form.
steps: From cos θ = a/ρ, solve for a by multiplying by ρ.
From sin θ = b/ρ, solve for b the same way.
Substitute into a + bi and factor out ρ: that's the trigonometric form ρ(cos θ + i sin θ).
Example: 2<sub>π/3</sub>. Since cos(π/3) = 1/2 and sin(π/3) = √3/2, we get 1 + √3 i.
cx-p2b.use: Rectangular form is best for adding and subtracting; polar form for multiplying, dividing, powers and roots.

cx-pprod.title: Product in polar form: multiply moduli, add angles
steps: Write both numbers in trigonometric form, with angles α and β.
The moduli ρ₁ and ρ₂ are real numbers: move them to the front.
Multiply the two brackets like binomials, with i² = −1, and group real and imaginary parts.
They are exactly the angle-sum formulas for cosine and sine! (the ones in the α ± β tab).
The result is a complex number with modulus ρ₁ρ₂ and angle α + β.
If α + β falls outside (−π, π], add or subtract 2π to get the principal argument: it's the same point.
cx-pprod.use: Multiplying = multiplying sizes and adding turns. That's why complex numbers are perfect for describing rotations.

cx-pquot.title: Quotient in polar form: divide moduli, subtract angles
steps: Dividing means finding the number q that, multiplied by w, gives z.
Write q = r<sub>φ</sub> and use the product rule: moduli multiply, angles add.
Two complex numbers in polar form are equal if they have the same modulus and the same angle (up to full turns of 2π).
Solving: r = ρ₁/ρ₂ and φ = θ₁ − θ₂.
cx-pquot.use: Dividing undoes the turn: sizes divide and angles subtract.

cx-pconj.title: Conjugate and inverse in polar form
steps: Write ρ<sub>θ</sub> in trigonometric form.
Conjugating flips the sign of the imaginary part. Since cos(−θ) = cos θ and sin(−θ) = −sin θ, that's the same as replacing θ with −θ.
Same modulus, opposite angle: ρ<sub>−θ</sub>.
For the inverse, write 1 = 1₀ (modulus 1, angle 0) and apply the quotient rule.
cx-pconj.use: The inverse points the same way as the conjugate, but with size 1/ρ: if z is far from the origin, 1/z is close to it.

cx-moivre.title: De Moivre's theorem
cx-moivre.summary: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ. Raising to n multiplies the angle by n.
steps: Raising to n means multiplying the number by itself n times.
By the product rule, the moduli multiply (ρⁿ) and the angles add (θ + θ + … = nθ).
If the modulus is 1, we get 1 to the n, which is 1: only the angle changes.
Written in trigonometric form, that's De Moivre's theorem.
Example n = 2: expanding the square on the left and matching real and imaginary parts gives cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ and sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
Example: 1 + i = √2<sub>π/4</sub>. To the 8th: (√2)⁸ = 16 and 8·π/4 = 2π, a full turn: the result is 16.
cx-moivre.use: Compute large powers without expanding binomials, and derive multiple-angle formulas (cos 3θ, sin 4θ…).

cx-rot.title: Multiplying by 1<sub>β</sub> rotates by β
cx-rot.summary: Multiplying by cos β + i sin β rotates the whole plane by β around the origin.
steps: The point 1 = (1, 0) becomes cos β + i sin β = (cos β, sin β).
The point i = (0, 1) becomes i cos β + i² sin β = −sin β + i cos β = (−sin β, cos β).
Both axes rotate by the same angle β, so the whole plane rotates by β.
With β = 90°, multiplying by 1<sub>90°</sub> = i takes the real axis to the imaginary one: a 90° turn.
Example from your notes: rotating 30° and then 90° is rotating 120°, with sin 120° = √3/2 and cos 120° = −1/2.
cx-rot.use: It's the basis of rotations in computer graphics, robotics and animation.

cx-euler.title: Euler's formula
cx-euler.summary: e<sup>iθ</sup> := cos θ + i sin θ. It's the exponential form of a phasor.
steps: It's a definition: it extends powers of e to imaginary exponents. θ is always in radians.
Its modulus is 1 by Pythagoras (sin²θ + cos²θ = 1): e<sup>iθ</sup> always lies on the unit circle.
Its argument is θ (if θ is in (−π, π]; otherwise θ plus or minus full turns of 2π).
Any complex number in polar form can be written ρ e<sup>iθ</sup>: the exponential form.
With θ = π we get e<sup>iπ</sup> = −1, Euler's identity, which puts e, i, π, 1 and 0 into a single formula.
cx-euler.use: With exponential notation, working with complex numbers is working with powers: e<sup>iα</sup>·e<sup>iβ</sup> = e<sup>i(α+β)</sup>.

cx-cossin.title: Sine and cosine as exponentials
cx-cossin.summary: Adding and subtracting e<sup>iθ</sup> and e<sup>−iθ</sup> isolates cos θ and sin θ.
steps: Euler's formula with θ.
Euler's formula with −θ. Since cosine is even and sine is odd, we get cos θ − i sin θ: the conjugate of e<sup>iθ</sup>.
Add them: the sines cancel, leaving 2 cos θ.
Divide by 2.
Subtract them: the cosines cancel, leaving 2i sin θ.
Divide by 2i.
cx-cossin.use: It turns products of sines and cosines into sums of exponentials, which are much easier to integrate and differentiate.

cx-eprop.title: Properties of e<sup>iθ</sup>
cx-eprop.summary: It behaves like an ordinary power: exponents add and multiply.
steps: In polar form, e<sup>iθ</sup> = 1<sub>θ</sub>. Multiplying adds the angles: that's adding exponents.
Raising to n multiplies the angle by n (De Moivre): that's multiplying the exponent by n.
With any moduli: the moduli multiply and the angles add.
cx-eprop.use: The exponent rules work just like with real numbers: e<sup>a</sup>·e<sup>b</sup> = e<sup>a+b</sup> and (e<sup>a</sup>)ⁿ = e<sup>na</sup>.

cx-roots.title: n-th roots
cx-roots.summary: Every z ≠ 0 has n n-th roots, with modulus ⁿ√ρ and angles (θ + 2πk)/n.
steps: We look for every w = r<sub>φ</sub> with wⁿ = z.
By De Moivre, wⁿ has modulus rⁿ and angle nφ.
Match moduli: rⁿ = ρ, so r is the real (positive) n-th root of ρ.
Match angles, but angles may differ by full turns: nφ = θ + 2πk. Solve for φ.
With k = n we're back at the angle for k = 0 (a full turn), so k = 0, 1, …, n − 1 is enough: there are n distinct roots.
Consecutive roots are 2π/n apart: they form a regular n-sided polygon centred at the origin.
cx-roots.use: Solve equations like zⁿ = c. In ℝ, x³ = 8 has only one solution; in ℂ it has three.

cx-root1.title: Example: the cube roots of 1
steps: Write 1 in polar form: modulus 1 and angle 0.
Apply the formula with n = 3. The real root of 1 is 1, so all of them have modulus 1.
k = 0: angle 0, the real root 1.
k = 1: angle 2π/3 = 120°. cos 120° = −1/2 and sin 120° = √3/2. This root is called ω.
k = 2: angle 4π/3 = 240°. It's the conjugate of ω, and also ω² (two 120° turns).
k = 3 would give 2π = 360°: back to 1. That's why there are only 3 roots.
cx-root1.use: The cube roots of unity form an equilateral triangle and show up when solving cubic equations.

cx-z38.title: Example: z³ − 8 = 0
cx-z38.summary: The solutions are 2 and −1 ± √3 i: the cube roots of 1 times 2.
steps: Isolate z: z is a cube root of 8.
Trick: since 8 = 2³, divide the equation by 8 to get (z/2)³ = 1.
So z/2 is a cube root of 1, which we already know.
Multiplying by 2: z = 2, z = −1 + √3 i and z = −1 − √3 i.
With the direct formula: 8 = 8₀, its real cube root is 2 and the angles are 0, 2π/3 and 4π/3. Same result.
cx-z38.use: In ℝ this equation only has the solution 2. In ℂ all three appear, on an equilateral triangle of radius 2.

cx-exp.title: Complex exponential e<sup>z</sup>
cx-exp.summary: e<sup>a+bi</sup> = e<sup>a</sup> (cos b + i sin b): modulus e<sup>a</sup> and angle b.
steps: It's defined so that e<sup>x+y</sup> = e<sup>x</sup> · e<sup>y</sup> still holds.
e<sup>a</sup> is a positive real and e<sup>bi</sup> is a phasor with angle b: the result is already in polar form.
The modulus of e<sup>z</sup> depends only on the real part of z.
The angle of e<sup>z</sup> is the imaginary part of z (plus full turns).
Adding 2πi adds a full turn and changes nothing: e<sup>z</sup> is periodic with period 2πi.
Example: e<sup>1 + iπ/2</sup> = e · e<sup>iπ/2</sup> = e · i.
cx-exp.use: It describes oscillations that grow or decay: the real part controls size and the imaginary part the turning (RLC circuits, springs).

cx-log.title: Complex logarithm
cx-log.summary: log z = ln|z| + i arg z. It has infinitely many values, 2πi apart.
steps: The logarithm of z is the number w you must put in the exponent to get z: e<sup>w</sup> = z.
Write w = x + yi. Then e<sup>w</sup> has modulus e<sup>x</sup> and angle y; z has modulus ρ and angle θ.
Match moduli: e<sup>x</sup> = ρ, so x is the natural (real) logarithm of |z|.
Match angles up to full turns: y = θ + 2πk. There are infinitely many logarithms, one for each k.
The principal logarithm Log z uses the principal argument Arg z ∈ (−π, π] (k = 0).
Example: −1 has modulus 1 and angle π, so Log(−1) = ln 1 + iπ = iπ. In ℂ, negative numbers do have logarithms!
cx-log.use: It lets you define complex powers as z<sup>w</sup> = e<sup>w·log z</sup> and solve exponential equations in ℂ.
